title: Activation lab: VPC quickstart - minimal TF patterns (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc is a short, hands-on activation lab for customer VPC onboarding with a bias toward the smallest safe Terraform surface area. Goal: give field onboarding engineers a repeatable, low-friction path to provision the minimal networking pieces we need to attach Redwood Private (control plane + inference nodes) into a customer VPC and validate traffic flows. This is intentionally opinionated — we prioritize a low blast radius, clear rollback steps, and a minimal TF module set that can be extended later.

Audience:
- Field/onboarding engineers doing first 1-3 customer activations
- SEs preparing quick demos or PoCs
- SRE/Infra engineers who will review handoffs

High-level constraints and assumptions:
- Customer provides a VPC in AWS (single account) or equivalent in other clouds. This quickstart focuses on AWS but calls out cross-cloud differences where critical.
- No host-level access required for initial onboarding (we use endpoints, peering, and controlled egress).
- Customer is willing to accept a small number of managed route table/SG/NACL changes during validation.
- This pattern is intended for greenfield or lightly restricted environments; regulated customers should follow full private-deployments playbooks.

Minimal architecture summary (what we create):
- A single VPC endpoint (Interface Endpoint) for control-plane connectivity (if customer blocks public egress).
- A dedicated subnet range /26 (or larger per throughput) for Redwood-managed endpoints and transit routing.
- Security Group for Redwood endpoints: tightly-scoped by CIDR and port list.
- Route table entries for a managed-range to route to a Transit/Peering connection.
- A small NAT Gateway or egress proxy for software updates if required (optional opt-in).

Why this minimal approach:
- Reduces required Terraform changes to 4 resources (subnet, SG, route, endpoint) in the common case.
- Allows easy rollback by removing the subnet/route or disabling the endpoint.
- Keeps the initial surface small for security reviews and internal approvals.

Terraform module notes (minimal / composable):
- Module: ri_minimal_vpc_activation
  - Inputs (minimal): customer_vpc_id, customer_public_subnet_ids (list), activation_subnet_cidr, allowed_controlplane_cidrs (list), aws_region, tenant_tag (string)
  - Outputs: activation_subnet_id, activation_sg_id, controlplane_endpoint_id, activation_route_id
- Design decisions:
  - Keep modules single-purpose and idempotent. The activation subnet is the only resource with lifecycle = create/ignore_on_destroy optional flag toggled by a var for audit customers.
  - Use AWS "aws_vpc_endpoint" (interface) for control plane traffic when customer egress is restricted; otherwise use NAT + public egress.
  - Avoid creating Transit Gateway in this quickstart; prefer VPC peering for single-account single-region setups. Transit/Shared networking is covered in the reference architecture doc.

TF patterns and snippets (conceptual):
- Use data sources to discover existing VPC tags rather than hardcoding IDs where possible to reduce mistakes.
- Minimal example (pseudocode):
  data "aws_vpc" "target" { id = var.customer_vpc_id }
  resource "aws_subnet" "activation" { vpc_id = data.aws_vpc.target.id cidr_block = var.activation_subnet_cidr tags = { Name = "ri-activation-${var.tenant_tag}" } }
  resource "aws_security_group" "activation_sg" { name = "ri-activation-sg-${var.tenant_tag}" vpc_id = data.aws_vpc.target.id ingress = [ { from_port = 443 to_port = 443 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = var.allowed_controlplane_cidrs } ] egress = [ { from_port = 0 to_port = 0 protocol = "-1" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } ] }
  resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "controlplane" { vpc_id = data.aws_vpc.target.id service_name = var.controlplane_service_name subnet_ids = [aws_subnet.activation.id] security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.activation_sg.id] private_dns_enabled = false }

Operational validation checklist (pre-deploy):
- Confirm the customer_vpc_id and no overlapping CIDRs with Redwood-managed ranges.
- Confirm required IAM/TF permissions: ec2:CreateSubnet, ec2:CreateSecurityGroup, ec2:CreateRoute, ec2:CreateVpcEndpoint, ec2:ModifySubnetAttribute.
- Confirm whether the customer requires KMS-wrapped keys for endpoint traffic (if so, capture CMK ARN).
- Agree on a short maintenance window for any route table changes.

Activation procedure (step-by-step):
1) Kickoff call (15 min): confirm CIDRs, egress policy, and approval owner. Capture contact and Slack channel.
2) Run a dry-run terraform plan and export the plan file for audit: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan.
3) Apply in staging/test VPC if available. If not, apply to customer sandbox VPC.
4) Verify resources are present: aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=ri-activation-${tenant}.
5) Control-plane handshake: from our control plane IPs (we provide list), attempt TLS handshake on port 443 to the interface endpoint DNS name (if endpoint) or to the activation subnet egress IP.
6) Functional verification: run a small inference request using a dedicated test API key and confirm logs show a successful session.
7) Latency and egress test: ensure RTT < accepted SLO for the customer tier (see below).

Validation commands (examples):
- aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=${vpc}
- curl -vk https://${controlplane_dns}/healthz --resolve "${controlplane_dns}:443:${endpoint_ip}"
- traceroute/tcping to control plane address to verify hop count

Rollback matrix (quick and safe):
- Immediate rollback (fast path): delete aws_vpc_endpoint.controlplane and aws_route.activation_route. This severs Redwood connectivity but leaves customer VPC intact.
- Gradual rollback: set security group ingress to 0.0.0.0/32 (no access) then destroy subnet.
- Audit-friendly rollback: mark resources with tag "ri_activation:disabled=true" and wait 5m before full destroy; useful for customers who require change windows.

Upgrade & patch plan (how to move from quickstart to production):
- Phase 0 (activation): minimal resources as above, single AZ subnet, 1 interface endpoint.
- Phase 1 (harden): convert interface endpoint to multiple AZ subnets, add NACL baseline, tighten SG egress, enable private DNS if customer approves.
- Phase 2 (scale): introduce Transit Gateway or VPC share for multi-account routing; replace single NAT with centralized egress proxies.
- Phase 3 (compliance): add HSM/KMS integration, immutable audit logs to central S3, and automated rotation for CMKs.
- Each phase has a small TF module to add resources without destroying the activation baseline. We recommend feature flags and canary rollouts controlled via variables.

Testing and SLOs (recommended):
- Connectivity SLO: control-plane handshake success rate >= 99.5% over first 72h of activation.
- Latency SLO: 95th percentile RTT from activation subnet to Redwood control-plane < 80ms for standard tier (adjust per region).
- Test cadence: continuous smoke test every 30s for first 48h, then every 5m during stabilization. Failure alerts to #onboarding-escalations.

Security considerations and checklist:
- Least-privilege SG rules: allow only control-plane CIDRs and customer admin CIDRs. Block all high-risk ports (22, 3389) unless explicitly allowed and logged.
- NACLs: optional; when used, keep stateless rules simple and mirror SG rules.
- DNS: prefer private hosted zone delegation instead of public DNS records when possible.
- KMS: if customer mandates KMS, ensure endpoint traffic uses CMK via encryption-in-transit and at rest for any persisted artifacts.
- Logging: enable VPC Flow Logs to an S3 bucket or CloudWatch with 90-day retention as default for onboarding phase.

Observability hooks we require from customer or install ourselves:
- VPC Flow Logs (enabled)
- Route table change alerts (CloudWatch/EventBridge rule)
- Endpoint health checks (we run external probes)
- Terraform plan artifacts stored in a shared bucket for 6 months

Notes on edge cases and common pitfalls:
- Overlapping CIDRs: if customer CIDR blocks overlap with our activation ranges, propose a /27 carve-out or use NAT-backed ephemeral egress via an approved proxy.
- Shared subnets: avoid placing activation resources inside customer-managed shared subnets; use a dedicated subnet to minimize side effects.
- Firewall appliances: many customers place NGFWs in front of subnets; we may need their team to add allow rules for the control-plane IP list.
- MTU issues: if customer uses jumbo frames (9001), we recommend testing KV/cache replication paths; some inference kernels behave poorly with mismatched MTU.

Handoff checklist (to customer and to SRE):
- Deliverable to customer: TF plan file, resource list, tags, activation window notes, rollback steps, and owner contacts.
- Deliverable to SRE: monitoring links, runbooks for endpoint failures, Terraform state location, and CFN/TF outputs.
- Post-activation follow-ups (within 7 days): confirm logs, cost impact review, and schedule Phase 1 hardening if agreed.

Runbook snippets for common incidents:
- Endpoint flapping: check Route table target, check ENI health in the activation subnet, confirm security group not rate-limiting. Quick mitigation: replace endpoint with new one in a separate subnet and switch route.
- High egress costs observed: temporarily move to customer-managed egress proxy with tokenized caching, and run Optimize suggestions for batching.

Open questions to resolve before GA pattern:
- Formalize our public list of control-plane egress IPs and publish a CIDR bundle.
- Standardize Terraform lifecycle semantics for activation subnets in audited customers.
- Define minimal logs retention policy acceptable to privacy-conscious customers.

Appendix: quick ticket checklist (copy/paste into JIRA)
- [ ] Confirm CIDR carveout and tag naming convention
- [ ] Customer approval for route table change window (date/time)
- [ ] Provide control-plane CIDRs and test API key
- [ ] Create TF workspace and run initial plan
- [ ] Verify connectivity and run smoke inference test
- [ ] Post-activation cost review scheduled

Appendix B: example tag naming convention
- Name = "ri-activation-${tenant_tag}"
- ri:owner = "private-deployments"

Notes to self: keep this doc short and push larger reference architecture content into 'vpc-reference-collection' (separate doc). This file is intentionally action-oriented for a single-session activation lab.
